Issue #368: performance: `ProtoArray.Prune()` has $O(N^2)$ worst-case descendant reachability

## Overview

`ProtoArray.Prune()` in `internal/forkchoice/protoarray.go` (lines 200-213) uses a fixed-point iteration loop to determine which nodes are descendants of `finalizedIdx` and should be kept during pruning. While this is effectively $O(N)$ under normal chronological block arrival, it degrades to $O(N^2)$ (or $O(\text{depth} \times N)$) when orphan blocks are back-linked, potentially freezing the node during finalization stalls.

## Current implementation

```go
keep := make([]bool, len(pa.nodes))
keep[finalizedIdx] = true
for changed := true; changed; {
    changed = false
    for i, node := range pa.nodes {
        if keep[i] || node.Parent < 0 || node.Parent >= len(pa.nodes) {
            continue
        }
        if keep[node.Parent] {
            keep[i] = true
            changed = true
        }
    }
}
```

The fixed-point iteration scans all nodes on every pass, repeating until no changes occur.

- **Expected behavior:** Blocks are typically appended chronologically, so parents have smaller indices than children. A single forward pass updates parents and then children in the same pass, converging in effectively $O(N)$ time.
- **Worst-case behavior:** Orphan blocks break the topological ordering guarantee. `OnBlock()` appends a parent-unknown block with `Parent = -1`, and `linkOrphanChildren()` later back-links it to a *higher* index, giving children smaller indices than parents. Each forward pass then resolves only one depth level, so a linear chain of depth $D$ in reverse-topological order requires $D$ passes over the whole array — $O(N^2)$ worst case.

## Pain

- `Prune()` runs on the Engine's single-threaded tick loop (`head.go`), so a slow prune stalls ticks → clock drift → missed duties.
- Under normal finalization the tree is small and the overhead goes unnoticed. During a finalization stall (stalled justified checkpoint, offline majority, adversarial forks), the proto-array can grow to thousands or tens of thousands of nodes before pruning fires.
- When finalization resumes, the massive $O(N^2)$ loop can lock up the CPU, causing the node to freeze, crash, or fall out of sync right when it needs to process blocks to catch up to head.

The $O(N^2)$ claim was validated by a reviewer, including a throwaway benchmark comparing linear chains with forward (parent-first) vs reverse (child-first) insertion, showing the reverse case requiring one pass per depth level (reverse back-edges). (Benchmark table values truncated in the issue.)

## Proposed Solution

Replace the fixed-point iteration with a single BFS or DFS rooted at `finalizedIdx`, guaranteeing strict $O(N)$ pruning:

1. Add a `children` index to `ProtoArray` (e.g., `map[int][]int`, or `Children []int` on `ProtoNode`).
2. Maintain the index incrementally — appending a child in `OnBlock()` and resolving orphans in `linkOrphanChildren()` costs $O(1)$ per insertion.
3. In `Prune()`, replace the fixed-point loop with a standard BFS/DFS queue initialized with `finalizedIdx`.

Walking the tree down via child pointers makes reachability $O(V + E)$, which is guaranteed $O(N)$ since the data structure is a tree.

## Notes

A reviewer confirmed the algorithmic claim (with "one important caveat on reachability") and opened a separate issue (#370) with a lighter-weight fix than the one proposed here.

Issue #340: [Initiative #329][EPIC #331][Phase #340] Build the implication graph and SCCs in Rust

## Overview
Implement a new self-contained `cdg` module in the Rust engine that derives Zsigmondy-forced residue classes for each prime-power component, builds a directed implication graph over component indices, and computes strongly connected components (SCCs) with an iterative Tarjan algorithm. In a second phase, extend `SearchBackbone` with this implication metadata and populate it during backbone construction, leaving existing pruning behavior untouched.

## Use Cases
- For each component, enumerate divisors `d > 1` of `2e+1` and derive the forced residue class `q ≡ 1 (mod d)`.
- Map forced residue classes to candidate component indices, producing per-component forced-candidate sets.
- Build an implication graph `i -> j` ("choosing component `i` forces candidate `j`") and compute SCCs over it.
- Surface forced-candidate sets and SCC lookup on `SearchBackbone` so downstream DFS phases can use them.

## Task 1: `cdg` module (Phase 1)

### Module setup
- Create `rust-engine/src/cdg.rs`.
- Register in `rust-engine/src/main.rs` as `mod cdg;` (plain `mod`, not `pub mod`), placed alphabetically before `mod distributed;` in the third module block.

### Forced residue classes and candidate mapping
- Helper enumerates divisors `d > 1` of `two_e + 1` (since `PrimePower.two_e` already stores `2*e`), using the `for d in 1..n { if n % d == 0 }` trial-loop idiom.
- For each divisor `d`, treat it as the modulus of the forced residue class `q ≡ 1 (mod d)`.
- Build a prime-to-component-index map from `components: &[PrimePower]`, e.g. `HashMap<u64, Vec<usize>>` keyed by `.p`, using `entry(...).or_insert_with(Vec::new).push(i)` (modeled on the `prime_counts` grouping in `math_utils.rs::composite_tonelli_shanks`). This replaces ad-hoc `.iter().rposition(...)` lookups.
- For each component `i` and each divisor `d > 1` of `two_e + 1`, collect candidate indices `j` where `components[j].p % d == 1`. Use a simple generic `p % d == 1` check — do not reuse the fixed-modulus `IsValidMod8`, `Mod3`, `Mod5`, or `Mod9` helpers.
- Expose per-component forced-candidate sets as `Vec<Vec<usize>>` indexed by component index.

### Directed graph and Tarjan SCC
- Build adjacency list `Vec<Vec<usize>>` over component indices; edge `i -> j` derived from the forced-candidate sets.
- Implement iterative Tarjan SCC as net-new code, with an explicit work stack instead of recursion (consistent with `dfs_tree.rs`). No external crates.
- Expose `component_index -> scc_id` array (`Vec<usize>` sized to `num_components`) and per-SCC member lists (`Vec<Vec<usize>>`), using the same positional index scheme as `SearchBackbone` and `active_mask`.
- Single public constructor: `Cdg::new(components: &[PrimePower]) -> Cdg`, running derivation and graph/SCC computation together, returning forced-candidate sets, adjacency list, and SCC lookup.
- Add `#[cfg(test)]` unit tests with small concrete component sets covering divisor enumeration, candidate mapping, and SCC grouping (modeled on `obstruction.rs` inline test style).

## Task 2: `SearchBackbone` integration (Phase 2)

### Struct extension (`rust-engine/src/backbone.rs`)
- Add fields for per-component forced-candidate sets and the SCC lookup (`component_index -> scc_id` array plus per-SCC member lists) produced by `cdg.rs`.
- Keep `compatibility_matrix`, `min_n_product`, and `num_components` unchanged; add new fields alongside, not in place.
- Use owned `Vec<...>` types so fields clone cleanly — `SearchBackbone` and related state are cloned and snapshot/restored during DFS.

### Population in `SearchBackbone::new`
- Reuse the existing O(n²) loop (lines 41–67) comparing every component pair `(i, j)`; determine implication edges using resolved `sigma_factors` and prime data already in scope (`comp_i`, `comp_j`, `pre_resolved_factors[i]`, `pre_resolved_factors[j]`).
- Precompute the divisor list of `two_e + 1` once per component `i`, outside the inner `j` loop; inside the inner loop, test `components[j].p % d == 1` for each `d > 1`.
- Assemble per-component forced-candidate sets from these pairwise results.
- After the loop, build the adjacency list and run Tarjan SCC by calling the `cdg` module constructor (or lower-level functions); store the SCC lookup on the struct.
- Do not modify how `compatibility_matrix` or `min_n_product` are computed or written — existing bit-setting and product logic must produce identical results.

## Pain
- Ad-hoc `.iter().rposition(...)` component lookups need replacing with the prime-to-index `HashMap`.
- Recursive SCC approaches are out; the explicit-stack Tarjan must be net-new with no external dependencies.
- Backbone fields are cloned/snapshotted during DFS, so new fields must be owned and clone-friendly.
- Backbone construction is hot; divisor lists must be hoisted out of the inner pair loop to avoid recomputation.

Issue #148: PRD: Add GCF (GCFormat) as an alternative response encoding format

## Overview

Add **GCF (GCFormat)** as an operator-selectable alternative response encoding format for the Infrahub MCP server, alongside the existing TOON (Token-Oriented Object Notation) format. TOON already reduced token cost versus JSON, but on realistic workloads — large inventories with `include_attributes=True`, wide schema kinds, and blast-radius traversals with many paths — responses still crowd out LLM reasoning context and inflate per-call cost. GCF is an AI-native wire format that upstream benchmarks measure at **25–29% fewer tokens than TOON** with equal-or-better model comprehension. Deployments that do nothing see zero change; opting in yields additional savings on every data-returning call.

## Use Cases

- Operator selects encoding via environment variable; TOON stays default when unset, so upgrades change nothing for existing agents/pipelines.
- Agent-facing payloads encoded in the active format:
  - `get_nodes` attribute results (`include_attributes=True`) — cheaper paging over large inventories.
  - `get_schema` kind detail — schema exploration stays cheap even for wide kinds.
  - `infrahub://schema/{kind}` resource payload — same savings as the tool path.
  - `find_paths` and `find_reachable` results — compact impact analysis over many paths/dependencies.
- Server instructions' "Data formats" section describes the configured format; `infrahub_agent`, `query_infrastructure`, and `explore_schema` prompts explain the active format; tool response descriptions remain accurate regardless of format.
- Startup log shows the configured response format for operator confirmation.
- Flag documented in configuration reference and capabilities documentation; generated compose file and server manifest include the new flag.
- Explicit non-goals / unchanged behaviors:
  - `get_nodes` display-label responses (default `include_attributes=False` mode) keep their natural shape as plain string lists.
  - `query_graphql` responses remain JSON regardless of the flag.
  - Oversized-response truncation remains byte-limited and format-agnostic (GCF payloads truncated the same predictable way as TOON).
  - New encoder dependency must be pure Python with **zero transitive dependencies** to keep the supply-chain surface minimal.

## Implementation Decisions

- Add a `response_format` field to `ServerConfig` (allowed values `toon` and `gcf`, default `toon`), set via the standard `INFRAHUB_MCP_*` environment variable prefix. Validation occurs at construction time (consistent with ADR 0006, configuration validation at the boundary): an unknown value fails server startup fast with a clear, actionable message rather than surfacing as garbled responses mid-session.
- Introduce one central encoding helper that owns (a) an encode function which dispatches on the configured format, so all structured tabular payloads encode through a single choke point — adding or retiring a future format becomes a localized change rather than a repo-wide sweep.
- Unit test suite parametrized over both formats, so a regression in either encoding path fails CI immediately.
- Document a token-savings comparison between TOON and GCF on representative Infrahub payloads, giving the team evidence to decide later whether GCF should become the default.

Issue #1495: Vendor migration: reference-code hierarchy engine, preflight data-loss register, and Axiell Calm as its first consumer

## Overview

Build a vendor migration layer for Heratio (currently greenfield — no source detectors, vendor field maps, or migration services exist). The core deliverables are: (1) a reference-code hierarchy engine as a reusable service, (2) a preflight data-loss register, (3) a closed transform vocabulary for mapping files, and (4) an Axiell Calm source detector and field map as the first consumer.

A parallel AtoM-tree session shipped Calm support (v3.106.52: a `calm` signature in `SourceDetector`, a `CalmMapping` for catalogue/authority/accession records), but **none of it should be ported to Heratio** — this issue requests the pieces neither tree has, built where they belong.

## Background: current state of `ahg-ingest`

`ahg-ingest` is a generic CSV wizard (configure, upload, map, validate, preview, commit):

- `IngestCommitRunner` commits through `InformationObjectService::create()` (`IngestCommitRunner.php:242`), which shifts siblings and sets `lft` — the existing path maintains the tree correctly.
- It sets **one** `parent_id` per session (`IngestCommitRunner.php:197`); every imported record lands under a single parent. No per-row hierarchy reconstruction exists.

## Scope

**In:**

1. **Reference-code hierarchy engine (a service).** Calm's tree exists only in `RefNo`: `GB 123 ABC/1/2` is the child of `GB 123 ABC/1`, and nothing else in the export carries structure. The engine must topologically sort so parents are written before children, synthesise missing intermediate levels where a depositor skipped one, and reject cycles. Per-row parent resolution during import produces orphans. The same engine serves Adlib and other structured-reference-code vendors.
2. **Preflight data-loss register.** Emit an artefact before any write naming every field that will be dropped, flattened, or folded.
3. **Closed transform vocabulary** for mapping files — identity, parse_date, split, lookup — no arbitrary evaluation, so a mapping file is data, not a code-execution surface.
4. **Calm source detector and field map** as the first consumer.

**Out:**

- Porting the AtoM plugin code; that tree keeps its own implementation.
- Any dependency on `github.com/matthewbrutonall/open-collections-migration-framework` (MIT, Python, three commits, proof-of-concept). Its two worthwhile ideas (items 2 and 3) are adopted; its code is not a dependency. Verified not derived from ours — the overlap is domain convergence.

## Heratio-specific constraints

**Assert closure membership, not existence, and not `lft`.** On heratio_dev, ids 1275114..1275122 ("[SYNTHETIC] POPIA demonstration set") have `lft = 0` and 0 rows in `information_object_closure`, yet exist and render HTTP 200 — inserted directly by a seeder (0 of 9545 records have NULL `lft`, so the write services aren't at fault). A bulk importer is exactly this kind of writer; this is the sharp hazard for migration work. Tests must assert a record is *in the tree*, not merely created.

**Read through `AhgCore\Services\HierarchyQueryService`** (closure-backed with automatic `lft`/`rgt` fallback, #1333) rather than touching `lft` directly. `lft`/`rgt` staleness is a known failure — it once made preservation packaging grab 1 record instead of a whole collection. A Calm load walks descendants constantly to place children under reconstructed parents, so it would reproduce that at scale.

**Authority records are links, not text.** Calm holds Persons, Corporate bodies and Places as separate record types with real relationships to catalogue entries; these must resolve to an actor, not be copied into an access-point string. Precedent for the loss: on RARI, four structured technique fields were flattened into Subjects and Genre, unrecoverably, with no record of the flattening — the motivation for the data-loss register.

**Mapping files must not carry enumerated values.** Every enumerated value comes from the Dropdown Manager, never a hardcoded list; a `lookup` transform resolves against `ahg_dropdown` and does not inline its own options.

## Explicit decisions required

- **Calm's `Piece` level** has no equivalent in Heratio's level vocabulary. The AtoM implementation folds it into Item, losing a depositor distinction. Whatever is chosen must be recorded as a decision (not a silent fold) and must appear in the data-loss register.
- **Dates carry a display expression alongside start and end.** Keep both: text only loses sortability; normalised only loses "circa 1890s".

## Acceptance

- A Calm export with a deliberately gappy `RefNo` set imports with every record reachable through the closure, including synthesised intermediate levels.
- A cyclic or self-referencing `RefNo` set is rejected before any write, not part-way through.

Issue #22: Broken Shader Using Loops When Optimizations ON

## Overview

Any SPIR-V shader containing a loop is corrupted by `respv::Optimizer::run` when the input was compiled with optimizations ON. The corrupted module fails `spirv-val` (`The following forward referenced IDs have not been defined: '35[%35]'`), and downstream drivers fail: NVIDIA segfaults inside `vkCreateComputePipelines`, Mesa lavapipe returns `VK_ERROR_UNKNOWN`.

## Root Cause

With optimizations on, a loop counter is not kept in memory; the loop header has an `OpPhi` meaning "counter is 0 on first pass, counter + 1 on later passes". Only that `OpPhi` reads the `OpIAdd` computing counter + 1. re-spirv does not count an `OpPhi` as a reader, so dead code elimination deletes the increment, leaving the `OpPhi` pointing at a nonexistent instruction.

Details:
- `Shader::parseData` skips the loop back edge at re-spirv.cpp:1974 (`if (labelId == continueLabelId) continue;`). Skipping the adjacency edge is correct, since `instructionAdjacentListIndices` feeds the topological sort in `Shader::sort` and the back edge would make the graph cyclic.
- But the same list also seeds `instructionOutDegrees` (re-spirv.cpp:2131), which dead code elimination reads. `optimizerReduceResultDegrees` deletes an instruction once its out degree hits zero, so an increment feeding only the loop header phi starts at zero and is removed.
- Deletion already subtracts back-edge references: the teardown at re-spirv.cpp:2332 passes `pIncludePhi = true`, so deleting an `OpPhi` reduces the degree of every operand it names, back edge included. It is subtracted but never added — an unbalanced count.

This resembles issues #17 and #20, but the cause is different: no constant conditions or branch pruning involved, just dead code elimination miscounting.

## Reproduction

```glsl
#version 460
layout( local_size_x = 64 ) in;
layout( binding = 0, std430 ) buffer Out { float vals[]; };
layout( push_constant, std430 ) uniform Params { int n; };
void main()
{
	for ( int x = 0; x < n; x++ ) vals[ x ] = 1.0;
}
```

```
glslc -fshader-stage=compute --target-env=vulkan1.2 -O min_loop.glsl -o min_loop.spv
```

`min_loop.spv` passes `spirv-val`. After `respv::Optimizer::run`, `%35` is deleted while `%41` still names it:

```
 %10 = OpLabel
 %41 = OpPhi %int %int_0 %5 %35 %11
       OpLoopMerge %12 %11 None
       OpBranchConditional %23 %11 %12
 %11 = OpLabel
       OpStore %32 %float_1
-%35 = OpIAdd %int %41 %int_1
       OpBranch %10
```

Loop shape does not matter: constant trip counts, `while` with `break`, and accumulate-only bodies all reproduce. A phi from `?:` does not, since it has no back edge. (A reproduction archive `min_repro.zip` is attached to the issue.)

## Proposed Fix

A patch (`respirv.patch`, attached) keeps the back edge out of the adjacency list so the topological sort still works, but counts it into the out degrees separately. Since phi deletion already subtracts these references (`pIncludePhi = true`), the count balances.

## Validation

Tested with eight compute shaders from a real project at `-O0`, `-O`, and `-Os`, plus the minimal repro:

| input | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 5 shaders with loops, at `-O` and `-Os` | invalid, no pipeline | valid, pipeline works |
| 3 shaders without loops, all levels | valid | valid, output byte for byte the same |
| all 8 shaders at `-O0` | valid | valid, output byte for byte the same |

Unoptimized input is untouched — a no-op for callers that never optimize — and dead loops are still removed with identical output. End-to-end confirmed in a real game on Godot 4.8.dev (`5ec4857b3`), NVIDIA 610.57.04, RTX 2070 SUPER: stock re-spirv segfaults in `libnvidia-glvkspirv.so` via `compute_pipeline_create`; patched runs correctly.

## Discovery Context

Godot Engine uses re-spirv on every shader before `vkCreateShaderModule` on Vulkan. Godot's own shaders are unaffected because it compiles them with the optimizer off: `godot/modules/glslang/register_types.cpp:126` default-constructs `glslang::SpvOptions`, and glslang defaults `disableOptimizer` to `true` (SPIRV/GlslangToSpv.h:50). The bug is reachable from anything directly handing optimized SPIR-V to `shader_create_from_spirv`.

Issue #5191: Reproducible label-aware augmentation artifacts in the computer-vision example

## Overview

Propose a small, self-contained example (or optional variant of the existing `examples/computer_vision` example) that makes a label-aware augmentation policy an explicit, versioned artifact in a ZenML computer-vision pipeline, using the `albumentationsx` package (imports as `albumentations`).

## Use Cases

- Reproducible object-detection pipelines: the augmentation policy and seed are part of the data lineage — changing either changes the training dataset even when the source dataset is unchanged.
- The current `examples/computer_vision` workflow (FiftyOne COCO export → Ultralytics training → model artifact versioning → inference → FiftyOne analysis) versions the exported dataset and model, but has no explicit augmentation-policy artifact or label-aware dataset-preparation step between them.
- Stochastic preprocessing needs sample-level randomness that stays stable regardless of sample or worker execution order.

## Proposed implementation

Bounded to two ZenML steps:

1. Build an AlbumentationsX pipeline and return `A.to_dict(pipeline)` as a normal ZenML `dict` artifact.
2. Reconstruct it with `A.from_dict()`, apply synchronized image and bounding-box transforms to the exported YOLO dataset, and return the resulting directory as a ZenML `Path` artifact for the existing trainer.

Core sketch:

```python
import albumentations as A

policy = A.Compose(
    [
        A.HorizontalFlip(p=0.5),
        A.RandomBrightnessContrast(p=0.2),
    ],
    bbox_params=A.BboxParams(
        coord_format="yolo",
        label_fields=["class_labels"],
    ),
)

policy_artifact = A.to_dict(policy)

# In the downstream dataset-preparation step:
policy = A.from_dict(policy_artifact)
sample = policy(
    image=image,
    bboxes=bboxes,
    class_labels=class_labels,
    invocation_seed=stable_sample_seed,
)
```

The sample seed is derived from a pipeline parameter and a stable sample identifier, so the generated dataset does not change merely because the orchestrator processes samples in a different order.

Resulting lineage:

```text
source dataset -> augmentation policy + seed -> transformed dataset -> trained model
```

No new ZenML integration, stack component, or custom materializer is needed — only existing materialization for `dict` and `Path`.

## Alternatives considered

- Leaving augmentation inside the training implementation: does not make the policy or transformed dataset separate lineage artifacts.
- A custom materializer for `A.Compose`: possible, but a serialized dict is simpler and uses existing ZenML primitives.
- Changing the current computer-vision example by default: unnecessarily disruptive; an optional step or separate example preserves the existing path.

## Constraints / dependency boundary

- Public `albumentationsx` package is AGPL-3.0-only; imports as `albumentations`.
- Importing it requires PyTorch, which is intentionally not pinned in its package metadata (users choose CPU/CUDA/MPS builds); the example would document that runtime choice rather than add a universal PyTorch pin.
- AlbumentationsX stays scoped to this example, not a ZenML runtime dependency.

## Priority

Low — nice to have. Contributor is willing to implement once maintainers confirm placement (optional branch of `examples/computer_vision` vs. standalone example).

Security audit of the project's dependency `xmldom` (release 4.0.41) flagged 3 vulnerabilities (alert IDs: `15daa12a-21fb-42e7-9b19-ee8490e8c788`, `82db6447-5761-4e0a-a23c-cd4293cf469d`, `fb6e2875-4db3-4092-89f6-1f0c23ec4399`). The issue calls for remediating these vulnerabilities in the dependency.

## Vulnerabilities

### 1. CVE-2021-32796 — Severity: MEDIUM (Score: 5.3)

- **Alert ID:** `15daa12a-21fb-42e7-9b19-ee8490e8c788`
- **Affected versions:** xmldom 0.6.0 and older
- **Description:** xmldom (a pure JavaScript W3C standard-based, XML DOM Level 2 Core `DOMParser` and `XMLSerializer` module) does not correctly escape special characters when serializing elements removed from their ancestor. This may lead to unexpected syntactic changes during XML processing in some downstream applications.
- **Fix:** Resolved in version 0.7.0.
- **Workaround:** Downstream applications can validate the input and reject maliciously crafted documents.
- **Reference:** https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-32796

### 2. CVE-2022-37616 — Severity: CRITICAL (Score: 9.8)

- **Alert ID:** `82db6447-5761-4e0a-a23c-cd4293cf469d`
- **Affected versions:** `@xmldom/xmldom` before 0.8.3 (Node.js)
- **Description:** Prototype pollution vulnerability in the function `copy` in `dom.js`, via the `p` variable. Note: the vendor states "we are in the process of marking this report as invalid"; however, some third parties take the position that "A prototype injection/Prototype pollution is not just when global objects are polluted with recursive merge or deep cloning but also when a target object is polluted."
- **Reference:** https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-37616

### 3. CVE-2022-39353 — Severity: CRITICAL (Score: 9.8)

- **Alert ID:** `fb6e2875-4db3-4092-89f6-1f0c23ec4399`
- **Description:** xmldom parses XML that is not well-formed because it contains multiple top level elements, and adds all root nodes to the `childNodes` collection of the `Document`, without reporting any error or throwing. This breaks the assumption that there is only a single root node in the tree, which led to issuance of CVE-2022-39299 as it is a potential issue for dependents.
- **Fix:** Update to `@xmldom/xmldom@~0.7.7`, `@xmldom/xmldom@~0.8.4` (dist-tag `latest`), or `@xmldom/xmldom@>=0.9.0-beta.4` (dist-tag `next`).
- **Workarounds (depending on use case):**
  - Instead of searching for elements in the whole DOM, only search in the `documentElement`.
  - Reject a document that has more than 1 `childNode`.
- **Reference:** https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-39353

## Remediation Direction

The flagged dependency release (4.0.41) bundles xmldom versions affected by all three CVEs. Addressing the CRITICAL vulnerabilities requires updating `@xmldom/xmldom` to at least 0.8.3 (CVE-2022-37616) and to `~0.7.7`, `~0.8.4`, or `>=0.9.0-beta.4` (CVE-2022-39353); the MEDIUM CVE-2021-32796 is fixed as of 0.7.0.

Issue #453: [CONTROL] INDEPENDENT REVIEW QUEUE — READ FIRST

## Overview

This issue is the single, append-only review queue ("Control Tower") for the Second Brain repository. Human shorthand command: `验算第二大脑`. Engineering posts `REVIEW_REQUEST/v1` tickets only after a bounded slice reaches its independent-review stop gate; the reviewer appends `REVIEW_RESULT/v1` results. Ticket identity is `(pr, exact_head)`.

## Queue model

- Requests are append-only exact-head tickets; a request is pending iff no later `REVIEW_RESULT/v1` exists for the same `(pr, exact_head)`. Remediation creates a new exact head and a new request.
- The reviewer must NOT guess from "latest open PR" — historical/frozen Draft PRs and parallel engineering lines may exist. Only registered exact-head tickets are in queue.

`REVIEW_RESULT/v1` schema:

```yaml
schema: REVIEW_RESULT/v1
project: SECOND_BRAIN
pr: <number>
reviewed_head: <sha>
verdict: ACCEPT | CHANGES_REQUIRED | BLOCKED
review_evidence_ref: <PR review/comment URL or id>
review_channel: GITHUB_APPROVE | EXACT_HEAD_COMMENT_ATTESTATION
reviewer_agent_id: GPT_INDEPENDENT_REVIEWER
independence_attestation: NO_PRODUCTION_CODE_OR_REMEDIATION_ON_REVIEWED_HEAD
```

## Same-account GitHub APPROVE limitation

All ChatGPT engineering/reviewer windows use the same linked GitHub account, so GitHub may reject formal APPROVE ("Review Can not approve your own pull request"). This limitation must not be bypassed or misrepresented. When formal APPROVE is mechanically unavailable, canonical acceptance evidence is:

1. An exact-head PR review COMMENT containing the independent architecture/adversarial review;
2. A matching append-only `REVIEW_RESULT/v1` with `ACCEPT` or `CHANGES_REQUIRED`;
3. Exact `reviewed_head` equality with the current PR head at review completion;
4. Reviewer role separation (reviewing window did not implement/remediate the head);
5. Fresh CI/current-main verification where required.

`EXACT_HEAD_COMMENT_ATTESTATION + REVIEW_RESULT/v1` is sufficient workflow acceptance evidence; it is not GitHub platform approval. A genuinely separate reviewer identity could later use `GITHUB_APPROVE` as stronger evidence, but it is not required.

## Reviewer procedure for `验算第二大脑`

1. Read this issue and all comments.
2. Compute pending exact-head tickets only.
3. Freshly verify PR head and current `main`; stale/moved heads fail closed.
4. Process serially by priority, then request time.
5. Read protocol_ref, source Issue, PR body/diff/tests/CI/prior review threads.
6. Perform independent architecture/adversarial validation; CI green is evidence, not acceptance authority.
7. Do not modify production code, remediate, or merge.
8. Attempt formal APPROVE only if GitHub permits; otherwise use exact-head COMMENT attestation without retry games.
9. Append `REVIEW_RESULT/v1` here.

## Mandatory finding carry-forward policy

Every exact-head review MUST return all materially useful findings regardless of verdict; `ACCEPT` is not permission to discard non-blocking observations. Review evidence MUST contain these sections (use `NONE_IDENTIFIED` when genuinely nothing to report; never invent filler):

1. **MUST_FIX_BLOCKERS** — only findings blocking current acceptance criteria, authority boundary, safety/fail-closed requirements, exact-head provenance, or bounded scope; each with failure path, affected surface, required bounded outcome, and closure evidence.
2. **SHOULD_CONSIDER / NON_BLOCKING_FINDINGS** — correctness, maintainability, observability, test-quality, documentation, provenance, architecture observations; guidance, not hidden blockers.
3. **FUTURE_OPPORTUNITIES** — follow-on capabilities, reusable abstractions, governance/risk improvements; state benefit and reason deferred; mark `NOT_CURRENT_BLOCKER` unless fresh evidence requires otherwise.
4. **REMEDIATION_GUIDANCE** — for `CHANGES_REQUIRED`, narrowest repair direction and what to preserve; remediation worker reads all findings, but only `MUST_FIX_BLOCKERS` are mandatory; non-blocking findings must not be silently promoted to blockers without fresh evidence.
5. **CARRY_FORWARD / NEXT-REVIEW CHECKS** — unresolved observations/invariants for the next reviewer; on remediation, mark prior blockers/findings `CLOSED`, `STILL_OPEN`, `SUPERSEDED`, or `NOT_APPLICABLE`.

Verdict semantics must stay clean: blockers decide the verdict; other findings are carried forward, never silently dropped or promoted.

## Use Cases

Review queue activity recorded in this issue (all on PR #452, issue #451, protocol R149_INDEPENDENT_REVIEW_PROTOCOL_V1, engineering signal `R149_TASK_RELEASE_IMPACT_COMPOSITION_GATE_READY_FOR_INDEPENDENT_REVIEW`):

Engineering evidence at request: PR mergeable/unmerged, exact-head dedicated CI green, Python 3.11 + 3.13 success, R149 19/19, retained Control Tower 197/197, no self-review/merge.
2. **First result** — `CHANGES_REQUIRED` on `de550c6...` (evidence `issuecomment-5414443426`), finding two P1 fail-closed blockers in `coordination/CONTROL-TOWER/task_release_impact.py` / `existing_work_items` → `_collision_analysis()` → `control_tower.classify_collision()`:
   - **P1 — incomplete active-work collision evidence can degrade UNKNOWN to O0/no-overlap**: `existing_work_items` mechanically requires only `task_id` and `owns_coherent_change_surface`; omitted path/interface/domain/authority surfaces become empty/default collections, so `classify_collision` can return `O0 / NO_MATERIAL_OVERLAP`. Missing collision evidence must remain UNKNOWN/NEEDS_REVALIDATION rather than being interpreted as no overlap.

Issue #4349: RecursivePlanner._buildSubGraph: validated PlanGraph result is discarded; raw nodes retain original (pre-trim) dependsOn

## Overview

In `packages/franken-planner/src/planners/recursive.ts`, the private method `RecursivePlanner._buildSubGraph` (lines 97–126) builds a sub-graph of tasks for recursive planning. It runs cycle/validity checking via `PlanGraph.fromTasks()`, but immediately discards the validated, sorted result and instead returns a graph built via `PlanGraph.createWithRawEdges()` from a nodes map populated from the **raw input tasks** — whose `dependsOn` arrays still include cross-graph (already-completed) dependency IDs that were deliberately stripped when constructing `tasksWithInternalDependencies`.

```ts
// Line 124 — result is discarded
PlanGraph.fromTasks(tasksWithInternalDependencies, { reason: 'recursive expansion' });
// Line 125 — uses the original nodes map, whose tasks still carry the FULL original dependsOn
return PlanGraph.createWithRawEdges(nodes, edges, 0, 'recursive expansion');
```

## Current implementation

- Lines 98–107: `nodes` map is populated directly from the raw input `tasks` array; task objects retain full original `dependsOn` arrays.
- Lines 110–123: `tasksWithInternalDependencies` is built with cross-graph dependency IDs stripped out; the trimmed `edges` map is correctly constructed.
- Lines 124–125: the validated `PlanGraph` from `fromTasks` is thrown away; the return value uses the untrimmed `nodes` with the trimmed `edges`.

## Pain

1. **Node/edge inconsistency:** any caller invoking `graph.getTask(id)` on the returned sub-graph receives a `Task` whose `dependsOn` lists dependencies **not present** in the graph.
2. **Stale data downstream:** scheduling is still correct because `RecursivePlanner._exec` (line 36) uses `graph.topoSort()`, which relies on edges only. However, callers such as the HITL exporter, plan serializers, or any code reading `task.dependsOn` from a node get stale/misleading data referencing absent dependencies.
3. **Wasted work:** the cycle-checked, properly-sorted `PlanGraph` from `fromTasks` is entirely discarded, defeating its purpose.

## Recommended Fix

Replace lines 124–125 with the validated result:

```ts
return PlanGraph.fromTasks(tasksWithInternalDependencies, { reason: 'recursive expansion' });
```

`tasksWithInternalDependencies` already contains correctly-trimmed `dependsOn` arrays, and the validated edge map is built alongside it, so `fromTasks` yields a fully consistent graph with no need for `createWithRawEdges`.

## Severity

**Medium** — data inconsistency between graph nodes and edges; manifests as stale `dependsOn` arrays visible to downstream consumers (HITL exporter, plan serializers, any code reading task metadata from the sub-graph).

Issue #32: Limits

## Overview

Define deterministic rejection boundaries for hostile, malformed, or pathological semantic artifacts. The runtime accepts externally supplied semantic packages, catalogs, dependency graphs, execution requests, request bindings, provenance graphs, execution bundles, and ZIP archives — so resource behavior becomes part of portable verification.

Core principle: invalid or unsafe artifacts fail deterministically **before** uncontrolled resource exhaustion.

## Resource dimensions

Define deterministic limits or bounded algorithms for:

**Archives**
- maximum archive size
- maximum archive entry count
- maximum individual uncompressed entry size
- maximum total uncompressed size

**Semantics**
- maximum semantic assertion count
- maximum symbol count
- maximum identifier length
- maximum canonical value length
- maximum canonical line length

**Graphs**
- maximum models in dependency closure
- maximum dependency depth
- maximum derivation depth
- maximum relational dependency depth
- maximum provenance traversal depth

**Relational**
- maximum dataset rows
- maximum JOIN output occurrences
- maximum GROUP_BY coordinates
- maximum groups
- maximum aggregation contributions

**Execution**
- maximum execution request count
- maximum binding count

## Security cases

**Archive attacks:** ZIP bomb, path traversal, `../` entry, absolute path, duplicate normalized path, case-normalization collision where relevant, oversized member, excessive entry count.

**Semantic graph attacks:** dependency cycle, derivation cycle, dataset cycle, extreme dependency depth, extreme fan-out, extreme provenance expansion.

**Relational attacks:** intentionally explosive many-to-many JOIN, repeated Cartesian expansion, unbounded intermediate relation, aggregation over pathological cardinality.

**Canonicalization attacks:** extremely large identifiers, extremely large scalar values, oversized canonical serialization, pathological decimal representations.

## Failure timing

Reject unsafe structures as early as possible. Prefer:

- parse / structural verification before semantic execution
- closure validation before model evaluation

where possible.

## Interoperability

- Limits that affect whether an artifact is accepted must be part of a declared verifier profile. Two runtimes claiming the same profile should not disagree because one silently allows a vastly larger artifact.
- Resource limits must not affect semantic identity of valid artifacts — an artifact does not gain a different semantic identity merely because it is close to a verifier limit.

## Temporary resources

Verification and extraction must clean up temporary materialization after both success and failure. Core principle: safety policy constrains admissible execution; it does not rewrite semantic meaning.

## Acceptance criteria

1. ZIP traversal is rejected.
2. Absolute archive paths are rejected.
3. Duplicate normalized archive paths are rejected.
4. ZIP bombs are bounded.
5. Archive entry count is bounded.
6. Individual uncompressed size is bounded.
7. Total uncompressed size is bounded.
8. Dependency cycles are detected safely.
9. Dataset cycles are detected safely.
10. Provenance traversal is cycle-safe.
11. Deep semantic graphs cannot cause uncontrolled recursion.
12. Explosive JOIN cardinality has a deterministic bound or guarded execution policy.
13. Canonical resource limits are documented/profiled.
14. Failure occurs before expensive execution where possible.
15. Limits do not alter semantic identity of otherwise valid artifacts.
16. Equivalent implementations reject the same over-limit conformance fixtures.
17. Verification leaves no temporary materialization behind after failure.
18. Verification leaves no temporary materialization behind after success.

The client call degrades to a no-op, so an author wiring a pipeline to call itself (or nesting calls past `MAX_CALL_DEPTH`) gets a clean canvas and discovers the problem only as a rejected save modal, instead of a live badge on the offending node.

## Current implementation

- `validateCallGraph` lives at `shared/src/engine/params.ts:3532`; invoked client-side via `validatePipelineDoc` (`params.ts:1931`).
- The canvas calls it with no options: `canvasDoc.ts:69` passes only `{ params, nodes, edges, containers }`.
- Reading the function's own guards on `main` at `588dea75`:
  - `selfId === undefined` ⇒ the direct self-call loop (`params.ts:3540-3545`) never runs;
  - `resolvePipeline === undefined || selfId === undefined` ⇒ early return at `:3546`, before the DFS.
- Therefore the client-side call returns `[]` **unconditionally**. Every other structural error in this validator already surfaces live; the call graph is the exception.

## Pain

- Authors see graph errors only as save rejections, not live diagnostics on the node that caused them.

## Proposed design — not a wiring job

Two halves of different difficulty; splitting them is likely the right build.

**(a) Self-call check — needs only `selfId`.** No resolver, no fetch, no async. The canvas already knows which version it is editing. Cheap, high-value: a node calling its own version is the easiest cycle to draw by accident and is fully answerable from browser-local data.

**(b) Transitive cycle + depth checks — needs a resolver, which is a nonexistent seam.** `PipelineResolver` (`params.ts:1941`) is **synchronous**: `(id) => Pick<PipelineVersion, 'nodes'> | undefined`. Server-side that's trivial from the DB; in the browser, callee versions are a network fetch away. Options:

- **Pre-resolve** — fetch the reachable call closure up front, hand the validator a warm synchronous map, re-fetch on call-target change. Keeps `validatePipelineDoc` synchronous and preserves ONE shared FE/BE validator (the property worth protecting). Cost: a cache to invalidate, plus a first-render ambiguity where a not-yet-fetched callee is indistinguishable from an unresolvable one — `:3562` already treats an unresolvable callee as *not analyzable* and silently continues, correct polarity on the server but a false all-clear in a UI.
- **Async validator variant** — forks the shared entry point; to be avoided unless (a) proves insufficient.

Recommendation: build (a) alone first — a real, unambiguous fix that makes (b)'s cost visible before committing to a resolver design.

## Scope

1. Pass `selfId` from the canvas so the direct self-call error surfaces live, anchored to the offending node rather than appearing as a save rejection.
2. Unit coverage that the client path now returns the self-cycle error where it previously returned `[]` — mutation-prove it (remove `selfId`, watch it go red).
3. Decide (b)'s shape explicitly in the PR body, settling the "unresolvable vs not-yet-fetched" ambiguity rather than inheriting it. If it needs more than a slice, file it.

- `ExpressionPicker` in `CallPanel` — #1012.
- The uncapped child-run list — #1235.

Issue #150: [P0][Roadmap] Qwen on M2: drive native decode toward 20–40 tok/s and speculative throughput toward 50–100 tok/s

## Overview

Drive the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Apple8 direct path on a 16 GB base M2 from ~2–2.5 tok/s native decode to a genuinely interactive local runtime. This is a performance program, not a promise of a specific token rate — continuously measure the hardware roofline and stop optimizing paths that cannot move the end-to-end token budget.

Target bands:

- **Native autoregressive decode:** 20–40 tok/s (stretch)
- **User-visible decode with MTP/speculation:** 50–100 tok/s (stretch)
- **Prefill/TTFT:** preserve large existing gains from direct Apple8 + MetalIO + prefix caching while decode is optimized

## Current validated baseline

The direct Apple8 runtime is model-output validated against the canonical-detile path on the M2.

### Prefill (direct raw Apple8 vs canonical-detile, fresh-process 63-token prompt)

- canonical TTFT: **165.645 s**; direct Apple8 TTFT: **11.738 s**; speedup: **14.11x**
- With 48/63-token prefix hit: canonical TTFT **44.264 s**; direct **3.644 s**; speedup **12.15x**; prefix restore ~**13–18 ms** for the process-local RAM tier

### Decode (the remaining problem)

Representative direct-path profiles show only **~2–2.5 tok/s**. A 2-token cached decode profile:

- wall: **970.7 ms / 2 tokens**
- routed expert requests: **320**; physical expert loads: **306**; expert cache hits: **14**
- expert I/O: **184.7 ms**; MoE: **421.0 ms**; GDN: **331.5 ms**; attention: **74.4 ms**; head: **52.1 ms**

Another direct run showed 320/320 routed expert loads for two tokens — essentially no useful decode residency.

Qwen's routed topology in these runs: top-k = **8**, roughly **20 routed MoE layers per token**, so about **160 routed expert applications per generated token**. The direct Apple8 path currently performs one expert operation at a time with synchronous GPU completion semantics — functionally correct but with huge dispatch/synchronization overhead.

## Hardware/roofline framing

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B activates ~3B parameters/token. Apple8 is ~4-bit-class storage plus per-row/group scale overhead → roughly **~1.5–1.7 GB of active weight data/token** if every active weight must be fetched from memory. On a base M2-class memory subsystem (~100 GB/s peak), the bandwidth-only ceiling is ~**60 tok/s** before accounting for GDN recurrent state, attention/KV traffic, router/top-k, dense/shared expert layers, lm_head, activations, Metal command submission/sync, cache misses/storage I/O, and imperfect bandwidth utilization.

Therefore:

- **50 tok/s native** means approaching the roofline extremely well
- **100 tok/s native** is not a credible default assumption for this model/hardware
- **50–100 tok/s user-visible** becomes much more plausible if MTP/speculative decoding yields >1 accepted token per expensive verification step

Keep this distinction visible in benchmarks and documentation.

## Use Cases / Performance strategy

### P0 — stop unnecessary expert loads

The old residency budget assumes ~**2 GB per expert slot**, but a raw direct Apple8 expert in the validated artifact is only about **1,671,168 bytes (~1.59 MiB)** before allocator/metadata overhead. Consequences:

1. previously produced pathological `resident cap=4 < topk=8` and exposed a real decode correctness bug;
2. still prevents the runtime from using available UMA for hot expert residency.

Replace the heuristic with target-native resident footprint accounting; experiment with materially larger caps (e.g. 16/32/48/64 where memory allows). Ultimately residency should be frequency/recency-aware rather than an equal-cap blind LRU. Goal: make MetalIO service the cold tail, not nearly every routed expert.

### P0 — fuse one routed MoE layer into a GPU wave

Current shape: per-expert load/wait → gate/up Metal work → wait → SwiGLU/down Metal work → wait → accumulate, i.e. ~**160 expert-level GPU interactions per token** at top-8 × ~20 routed layers. Target shape:

```text
router -> top-8
       -> acquire/pin/load required expert slots
       -> one Metal command buffer / layer
          - 8 gate/up projections
          - SwiGLU
          - 8 down projections
          - weighted reduction
       -> next layer
```

First milestone: reduce expert-level synchronization to roughly **one MoE synchronization per layer (~20/token)**. Later: encode multiple layers before host synchronization where dependencies permit.

### P0 — move Gated DeltaNet decode to Metal

Mandatory for the 50 tok/s program. Representative decode profiling shows **145–165 ms/token** in GDN alone; a 50 tok/s target has a total token budget of only **20 ms**, so 50 tok/s is mathematically impossible while GDN stays near its current cost. Implement a native Metal GDN decode path with recurrent state resident in UMA/GPU-visible memory, fusing input projections, causal convolution update, delta recurrence, gating/normalization, and output projection as practical.

Instrument first:

P0 Milestones:

- [ ] #151 — target-native residency budgeting + hot expert policy: remove 2 GB/slot heuristic; normal M2 config should resolve to cap ≥ top-k when memory permits; drive physical expert loads/token down sharply
- [ ] #152 — fused top-k Apple8 MoE layer: depends on safe leases/transient slots from #151; target roughly one routed-MoE host synchronization per layer instead of per expert
- [ ] #153 — native Metal Gated DeltaNet decode: can proceed in parallel with #151/#152

## Milestone C verdict (falsified premise)

Milestone C (whole-token Metal, #154) sync-elimination premise is falsified on the M2. Measured bisect (commit 3cf7edd): whole-token kernel runs **75–80 ms per layer GPU** vs **4 ms per layer** for the per-layer path. Even a perfect whole-token kernel (~160 ms/token GPU) cannot beat the per-layer path (**161 ms/token wall**, CPU/GPU pipelined). **GPU compute is the bottleneck, not host syncs.** The whole-token path stays as a token-identical correctness reference (it caught the GQA rep=2 bug), default off.

Roadmap implication: decode speedups must come from faster kernels (fused MoE #152, native GDN #153), not fewer dispatches.

Issue #243: RI3.7: Enforce relationship authority across impact, tests, planning, contracts, and verification

## Overview

Issue RI3.7 (parent #236, depends on #237/#238, integrates with #239/#240) makes the proof/authority distinction operational across every downstream feature that can influence an autonomous code change. Adding proof metadata is insufficient if impact analysis, test selection, planning, architecture policy, contracts, or verification still treat heuristic and authoritative relationships as equivalent. The issue establishes one shared downstream relationship-consumption policy and removes implicit trust of unproven graph edges.

## Core rule

```text
authoritative relationship
    -> may justify constraints, impact, required validation, contract boundaries

corroborating relationship
    -> may raise confidence / ranking, but cannot independently justify a hard claim

heuristic relationship
    -> retrieval/context suggestion only; cannot create hard downstream obligations or certainty
```

## Shared consumer policy

Add a centralized policy/helper layer, conceptually:

```rust
pub struct RelationshipUsePolicy {
    pub minimum_authority: RelationshipAuthority,
    pub accepted_proof_kinds: Option<BTreeSet<RelationshipProofKind>>,
    pub allow_ambiguous_candidates: bool,
    pub ambiguity_behavior: AmbiguityBehavior,
}
```

or equivalent reusable methods over the existing graph/query APIs. Do not duplicate authority checks separately in every crate.

## Impact analysis

Update impact traversal so:

- authoritative `CALLS`, `REFERENCES`, `USES_TYPE`, `IMPLEMENTS`, `EXTENDS`, and dependency edges can expand structural impact;
- corroborating edges may adjust ranking/confidence but do not independently expand a hard blast radius unless an explicit policy says so;
- heuristic/fuzzy relationships do not become structural impact paths;
- ambiguous relationships are surfaced as possible impact/caveats, not definite affected nodes;
- each impact path explains the relationship proof(s) that justified traversal.

Add a distinction in output between `proven_impact` and `possible_impact` without breaking existing clients; use additive fields/versioned detail where needed.

## Test selection

Required/strongly recommended tests must be justified by authoritative or explicitly accepted corroborating evidence such as:

- authoritative dependency/call/reference path;
- exact coverage evidence;
- exact test ownership/mapping;
- strong history/runtime evidence under existing policies.

A fuzzy structural relationship alone cannot turn a test into `required`. Heuristic candidates may be retained as lower-priority optional suggestions.

## `plan_change`

Plans must distinguish:

- proven edit/impact boundaries;
- possible/ambiguous relationships;
- missing proof that lowers confidence;
- evidence families required before a hard recommendation can be made.

Do not present a heuristic call/reference edge with language implying certainty. Where task policy requires structural evidence and only heuristic relationships exist, surface a blocker/caveat per existing Context Compiler fail-closed rules.

## Architecture policy

Architecture dependency violations must rely on authoritative dependency/import/reference relationships per policy semantics. Heuristic relationships may be shown as potential violations requiring confirmation, but cannot alone produce an enforce-level violation. Every enforceable violation should identify: policy rule; source/target; relationship authority; proof IDs/kinds; source range when available.

## Change contracts

Contract construction must record whether each boundary/affected dependency is `proven`, `corroborating`, or `possible`. Hard contract constraints derived from repository relationships require authoritative proof unless a different evidence family independently establishes the constraint. Boundary expansion based only on heuristic graph candidates must require explicit evidence/confirmation rather than silently widening the contract.

## `verify_change`

Verification must not claim a relationship violation or successful preservation from heuristic graph truth. When comparing before/after graphs:

- compare authoritative relationships as contract/verification facts;
- track corroborating/heuristic relationship deltas separately;
- surface newly ambiguous/unresolved relationships as evidence-quality regressions where relevant;
- preserve proof traceability for changed relationships.

## Context Compiler

Candidate streams may continue to use all evidence classes for retrieval, but fusion/selection must preserve authority:

- heuristic candidates may improve recall;
- they cannot be re-labeled authoritative through fusion score;
- exact/proven relationships keep authority regardless of numeric ranking;
- ContextPack diagnostics record authority mix and ambiguous relationship count.

## Proof-path explainability

For hard downstream claims, expose a compact proof path, e.g.:

```text
OrderService.save
  --CALLS [ExactCallSite + ReceiverType]--> Repository.persist
  --REFERENCES [ExactReference]--> OrderRecord
```

The path must preserve evidence IDs/ranges so agents can inspect source rather than trusting an opaque score. Cap path length/output using existing MCP pagination/result-limit conventions.

## Confidence model

Do not simply map `authoritative = confidence 1.0`. Authority answers whether the relationship is structurally proven under current semantics; confidence may still capture additional uncertainty separately from authority.

Issue #2320: cl: make recursive runtime.Caller reachability order-independent

## Overview

In the `cl` (compiler/linker) analysis pass, `runtimeCallerAnalysis.fnMayReachRuntimeCaller` can produce an order-dependent false result for functions inside a recursive call cycle. The result is memoized, so if DFS reaches a function already in the `visiting` set it returns `false`, and that provisional result can be cached for a cycle member before another member's direct `runtime.Caller` edge is visited.

Minimal reproducing shape:

```go
package cycle

import "runtime"

func a() {
	b()
	runtime.Caller(0)
}

func b() {
	a()
}
```

If `a` is analyzed first, the `a -> b -> a` back-edge causes `b` to be memoized as `false` before `a` reaches `runtime.Caller`. If `b` is analyzed first, both functions are classified correctly. The starting function is chosen via map iteration, so the outcome is nondeterministic.

## Use Cases

- Correctly classifying all functions in a recursive SCC as able to reach `runtime.Caller`, so caller-frame tracking does not under-approximate.
- Deterministic analysis results independent of map iteration order.

## Pain

- A local probe rebuilding and analyzing the above package 100 times omitted `b` from `computeRuntimeCallerBaseSet` in 79 runs.
- Because caller-frame tracking can under-approximate recursive SCCs, a frame that can actually reach `runtime.Caller` may be inlined or tail-called, breaking runtime-visible behavior.
- Results vary run to run due to map iteration order, making the bug flaky and hard to test.

## Current implementation

`fnMayReachRuntimeCaller` performs a DFS with a `visiting` set; encountering a node already in `visiting` returns `false` (treated as "does not reach"), and results are memoized per function. This memoization of a provisional cycle-local result is the source of the incorrect classification.

## Suggested direction

- Compute reachability to caller consumers as a graph fixed point, or over strongly connected components, so that a positive `runtime.Caller` edge propagates through the entire recursive component.
- Add a regression test that repeats analysis with controlled visitation orders rather than relying on randomized map iteration.

This behavior predates #2293 and was identified during its review; it should be fixed separately to keep the #2293 PR scoped to recover-visible panic-site tracking.

Issue #508: Diamond task dependencies falsely rejected as circular in run, lanes run and lanes validate

## Overview

In `fledge`, a **diamond dependency** — two tasks sharing a common dependency (e.g. `test` and `lint` both depending on `build`) — is falsely reported as a circular dependency and hard-fails. Three commands are broken: `fledge run`, `fledge lanes run`, and `fledge lanes validate`. No cycle exists in the repro; the graph is a DAG.

## Reproduction

`fledge.toml`:

```toml
[tasks]
d = "echo d"

[tasks.b]
cmd = "echo b"
deps = ["d"]

[tasks.c]
cmd = "echo c"
deps = ["d"]

[tasks.a]
cmd = "echo a"
deps = ["b", "c"]

[lanes.build]
description = "diamond deps, no cycle"
steps = [{ task = "a" }]
```

Graph: `a → [b, c]`, `b → [d]`, `c → [d]`. A DAG; `d` has no dependencies at all.

Observed failures:

```
$ fledge run a
error: Circular dependency detected: task 'd' depends on itself

$ fledge lanes run build
error: Lane 'build' failed at step 1 (a) after 1ms: Circular dependency detected: task 'd' depends on itself (chain: c → a → d → b)

$ fledge lanes validate
error: Circular dependency detected involving task 'a'
error: Validation failed
```

Notably, `fledge lanes run build --dry-run` **passes** because it uses the one correct implementation — dry-run and real run disagree.

`d` is a bare string task with no `deps` key, so "task 'd' depends on itself" is impossible on its face. The `chain:` in the lane-run message is a `HashSet` iterated in arbitrary order, not an actual path — `c → a → d → b` is not a walk in this graph.

## Root cause

There are **four** cycle detectors. One is correct; three share the same defect:

| Location | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `src/lanes/mod.rs:506` `check_dep_cycle` | **Correct** — `visiting.remove(name)` after recursing (proper backtracking) |
| `src/run.rs:282` `execute_task` | Buggy — `visited` accumulates, never removed |
| `src/lanes/execute.rs:384` `execute_task_recursive` | Buggy — same |
| `src/lanes/validate.rs:122` `validate_lanes` | Buggy — same, iterative variant |

The three buggy ones conflate two distinct sets:

- **"currently on the recursion stack"** — revisiting this *is* a cycle.
- **"already completed"** — revisiting this is just a shared dependency, and should be skipped, not rejected.

`check_dep_cycle` removes the node on the way out, so it works. The others keep one accumulating `visited` set, so the second path into any shared node is misread as a cycle. In `run.rs` the same set also does double duty as run-once dedup, tangling the bug with dedup logic.

## Suggested fix

Use two sets (or one set plus backtracking):

- **Cycle detection**: an on-stack set, inserted before recursing and removed after — i.e. what `check_dep_cycle` already does.
- **Run-once dedup**: a separate `completed` set that is only ever added to; a hit means "skip, already ran", not "error".

Given `check_dep_cycle` is already correct and already used by the dry-run path, the cleanest fix is to delete the three duplicates and have all callers use it, keeping a separate `completed` set in the two executors for dedup.

## Test coverage gap

`validate_lanes` has no unit tests — the existing `validate_circular_deps` test exercises `check_dep_cycle`, the one implementation that isn't broken. Regression tests should assert that a diamond **passes** in all four paths, and that a genuine cycle (`a → b → a`) still fails in all four.

## Impact

Any project whose task graph has a shared dependency cannot run it. Sharing a `build`/`setup` task between `test` and `lint` is a normal pattern, and `--dry-run` disagreeing with the real run makes this confusing when hit.

(Found while re-scoping #446; posted separately as a shipped correctness bug rather than a cleanup.)

A maintainer on the project sourcenetwork/defradb (Go) filed this issue about hand-rolled graph machinery causing pain:

Issue #5135: Counter over-counts: loadComposites re-walks diamond ancestors, applying the same block delta twice in one merge

## Overview

`mergeProcessor.loadComposites` can push the same composite block onto `mp.composites` more than once within a single merge, and `ProcessBlock` then calls `crdtData.Merge` once per occurrence. For a `P_COUNTER` field, whose `Merge` is a pure read-modify-write, the increment is applied twice and the counter over-counts. The bug reproduces deterministically on a single node — no P2P, no concurrency, no second implementation involved.

## Root cause

`internal/db/merge.go`, `loadComposites`. Its doc comment says it retrieves composite blocks for a CID "until it reaches a block that has already been merged or until we reach the genesis block", but the implementation has **no visited set and no already-merged check**. The only stop conditions are `mt.heads[blockCid]` and the priority walk-back branch. When a block has two parents that reconverge on a shared ancestor (an ordinary diamond), the recursion descends into that ancestor once per path and pushes it twice.

`internal/core/block/store.go` `ProcessBlock` then merges unconditionally:

```go
if err := crdtData.Merge(ctx, block.Delta.GetDelta()); err != nil {
    return NewErrMergingDelta(blockLink.Cid, err)
}
```

and `internal/core/crdt/counter.go` `Merge` is a pure RMW, so repeated application is not idempotent. LWW and composite deltas are idempotent under repeated apply, which is why this surfaces as a counter bug specifically.

The CID guard in `internal/db/p2p/p2p.go` (`processQueue` / already-processed check) only covers the *inbound head* CID; it does not help when an already-applied interior block is re-walked as part of a later merge.

## Reproduction

Four tests written against `v1.0.0` (`3de01484`) in the idiom of existing `internal/db/merge_test.go` helpers:

| Scenario | Expected | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| Diamond above a divergent head | 5 | **6** |
| Minimal unmerged diamond, no local branch | 4 | **5** |
| Three stacked diamonds | 9 | **21** |
| Control: same blocks, one merge event at a time | 4 | 4 (passes) |

The stacked-diamond case compounds per level, so deep DAGs amplify rather than produce off-by-one — consistent with the runaway counter values reported in #4935.

**The control is diagnostic.** Delivering the same blocks one `event.Merge` at a time passes because every shared ancestor is already in `mt.heads` by the time the reconvergence block arrives. The bug is therefore sensitive to how many new blocks arrive in a single merge (delivery batching under load), not to timing or races — which explains why it has appeared intermittent and environment-dependent.

Tests use existing helpers (`newDagBuilder`, `generateCompositeUpdate`, `generateCounterCompositeUpdate`, `newBadgerDB`, `userSchemaWithCounter`) plus two added variants: `generateCounterCompositeUpdateNonce` (nonce-parameterised, so sibling increments of equal value are content-distinct) and `generateCounterCompositeUpdateFromHeads` (builds a block with two parents).

## Pain: why the suggested fix in #4935 doesn't work

Guarding with `IsMerged` inside `ProcessBlock` does **not** work. `IsMerged` (`internal/datastore/blockstore.go`) means "present in the blockstore and absent from the to-merge index", and that index is only written by `p2pBlockStore.Put`. Locally authored blocks go through `Multistore.Blockstore()`, which never adds them, so a locally written block reads as already-merged the moment it is stored. Adding an `IsMerged` gate to `loadComposites` breaks 10+ existing merge tests. PR #4936 also would not have addressed this path: it filters non-composites, and the block applied twice here *is* a composite.

## Fix that worked

An applied-marker keyed by **(CRDT headstore prefix, block CID)**, checked and set around the `Merge` call in `ProcessBlock`:

```go
scope := crdtData.HeadstorePrefix().Bytes()
applied, err := isDeltaApplied(ctx, scope, blockLink.Cid)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
if !applied {
    if err := crdtData.Merge(ctx, block.Delta.GetDelta()); err != nil {
        return NewErrMergingDelta(blockLink.Cid, err)
    }
    if err := markDeltaApplied(ctx, scope, blockLink.Cid); err != nil {
        return err
    }
}
```

Results: `go test ./internal/db/... ./internal/core/...` fully green including the four new tests; a mixed-cluster counter storm went from over-counting in 5/5 runs to 0/6.

**The doc+field scoping is load-bearing.** A CID-only marker breaks `TestBackfillIndex_NonRetryableError_MarksFailed`, because two different documents can produce byte-identical field deltas and therefore the same CID; scoping to the headstore prefix keeps them distinct.

An alternative fix — deduping inside `loadComposites` with a visited set — would also stop the double-push and may be more natural, but was not tested and cannot be vouched for.

## Scope & context

Present at `v1.0.0` (`3de01484`); `git diff 3de01484 develop` on `internal/db/merge.go`, `internal/core/block/store.go`, `internal/core/crdt/counter.go` is empty as of `13c46ec9`, so `develop` is unaffected by intervening changes.

Found via cross-implementation testing between the Go DefraDB and a Rust reimplementation, which produced different counter values from byte-identical input.

Maintainer note (jsimnz): the blockstore already maintains a `merged` marker at the kv level via `MarkAsMerged`; the fix is likely just a missing branch to check the merged index *before* the `Merge` call.

Issue #4184: RecursivePlanner._buildSubGraph discards validated fromTasks result, returning an unordered raw-edge graph

## Overview

In `packages/franken-planner/src/planners/recursive.ts` (lines 97–126), `_buildSubGraph` calls `PlanGraph.fromTasks()` only for its validation side-effect (cycle detection + topological sort) at line 124, then discards the return value. The graph actually returned on line 125 is built via `PlanGraph.createWithRawEdges(nodes, edges, 0, 'recursive expansion')`, which bypasses topological ordering entirely.

## Current implementation

```ts
// Line 124 — return value is discarded!
PlanGraph.fromTasks(tasksWithInternalDependencies, { reason: 'recursive expansion' });
// Line 125 — actual return uses the raw, unordered graph
return PlanGraph.createWithRawEdges(nodes, edges, 0, 'recursive expansion');
```

## Pain

1. **Validated, topologically-sorted graph is thrown away.** `RecursivePlanner._exec` calls `graph.topoSort()` on the returned graph, so in practice the re-sort compensates — but any structural difference between the raw `nodes` Map insertion order and the topologically correct order is silently corrected at execution time rather than at build time.
2. **Wasteful validation.** If `fromTasks` throws `CyclicDependencyError`, the exception propagates correctly, so cycle detection still works — but the correctly sorted graph is immediately discarded and reconstructed from raw edges, making the cycle-detection-only path confusing and fragile.
3. **Silent divergence risk.** If future code paths consume the returned graph's task order before calling `topoSort()` (e.g. iterating `getTasks()`), they receive tasks in arbitrary insertion order rather than dependency order.

## Fix

Replace lines 124–125 with a single call to `PlanGraph.fromTasks` and return its result:

```ts
return PlanGraph.fromTasks(tasksWithInternalDependencies, { reason: 'recursive expansion' });
```

This eliminates the redundant double-graph construction and ensures the returned sub-graph is both validated and topologically ordered.

Issue #192: [spec] 发布 Native Hook protobuf data/config Source tables

## Overview

Formal `kat import hitrace` currently does not publish Native Hook payload Source tables, while the old query path's hand-written Native Hook tables are not a long-term Data Import Source-table contract and cannot prove that deep presence, oneof, repeated fields, and parent-child relationships are not omitted. PACK development environments and Hitrace Import may be physically isolated, so PACK authors cannot request that a Datasource add a deep protobuf field on demand; they need a complete, queryable source surface that is not arbitrarily trimmed to current Workflow needs.

The legacy PR #107 covers only a partial surface for a fixed-result plugin and depends on Dataset, directory, and clock contracts that have since changed, so it cannot be resumed or merged directly.

"Complete" has a clear boundary: it means the decoded semantics expressible by the protobuf descriptor closure explicitly bound to the current KAT — not raw wire archives, arbitrary user schemas, or cross-KAT-version compatibility promises.

## Solution

In formal Hitrace Import, publish Native Hook's `BatchNativeHookData` (data root) and `NativeHookConfig` (config root). At build time, a unique relational plan is produced from canonical protobuf FQNs; the same plan generates both the Arrow Schema and a typed emitter. At runtime, typed protobuf decode happens exactly once, then rows are written directly into sparse Source tables.

Every successfully bound profiler payload keeps an independent envelope occurrence; the payload root and all descendant relations recover origin, presence, oneof selection, and repeated ordering via relation keys within the current Dataset. Source tables are published via existing Dataset Storage and queried directly by DataFusion — no new catalog, manifest, runtime reflection, or second Import API.

The approach uses the prototype-validated "B′ seam": build-time relational plan plus generated direct emit. PRs #107, #119, and #175 serve only as sources of test, proto, writer, and performance evidence — no wholesale rebase or port of the old architecture.

## Delivery Plan (per maintainer comment)

Not resuming old PR #107; instead a new vertical path from current `main`:

1. **#194**: generic descriptor-to-Parquet engine, plus committing accepted ADR-0061; no production Import change.
2. **#195**: use the engine to generate complete dormant Native Hook data/config capture; still no production Import change.
3. **#196**: atomically enable four routes in formal `kat import hitrace`, and complete real-sample differential and release performance acceptance.

Three PRs: #194 (engine + ADR), #195 (dormant capture), #196 (formal enablement + differential + performance evidence).

## Use Cases

- **PACK authors**: full decoded source fields published once at Import, enabling independent analysis development without Datasource access; source tables not trimmed to current Workflow field needs.
- **KAT users**: obtain Native Hook Source tables via formal `kat import hitrace`; unregistered plugins remain explicitly reported; decode/emit/write failures on a bound payload fail the whole Import, with no identifiable partial Dataset left behind when failure occurs before publication.
- **Queryers**:
  - Each data/config payload connects to its originating profiler envelope (provenance).
  - Empty data root and all-default config root still keep occurrences (payload-exists-but-empty ≠ payload-absent).
  - proto3 implicit scalar defaults preserved per decoded semantics.
  - Explicit-presence scalars distinguish absent vs. explicit default; singular messages distinguish absent vs. present-but-default.
  - Scalar/enum/bytes oneof variants via nullable typed columns (distinguish unselected vs. selected-default); message-valued oneof variants via their own typed relations (no discriminator or generic value column).
  - Repeated scalars, bytes, enums, and messages preserve parent and element order for lossless reconstruction.
  - `bytes` preserved byte-for-byte (no implicit UTF-8/JSON/int-array conversion).
  - Enum occurrences keep original numbers (unknown enum numbers not dropped) and connect to the current descriptor's full symbol definitions.
  - Envelope `clock_id` interpreted only as raw source enum, not as normalized KAT time.
  - Descriptor-derived tables coexist with normalized facts like `sched_switch` under distinct names.

## Key Contract Points

- First slice binds two canonical FQN roots: `kat.native_hook.BatchNativeHookData` and `kat.native_hook.NativeHookConfig`; data and config must both be covered.
- Route binding: `nativehook` and `hookdaemon` data routes → Batch root, root table `batch_native_hook_data`; `nativehook_config` and `hookdaemon_config` config routes → Config root, root table `native_hook_config`. Route knowledge stays in a private sealed binding.
- Contract scope: known field values, explicit presence, oneof selections, repeated elements and order. Out of scope: unknown wire fields, raw encoding, wire field order, proto3 implicit scalar wire presence.
- `profiler_payload_occurrence` is a controlled provenance projection of the profiler transport envelope, not a registered protobuf root, and does not enter the descriptor relational plan. A private capture adapter exclusively owns its fixed eight-column schema, typed row, logical byte estimation, `ClockId` descriptor symbols, enum origin binding, and relation slot; callers only submit successfully bound envelopes and write roots through the adapter, never touching relation vectors, slots, or origin specifications directly.
- Relation keys are Dataset-local structure only — not cross-Import stable identity.
- All tables continue to honor existing Dataset Storage and logical table name contracts (resolver, inspection, DataFusion query).

## Maintenance / Build-Time Guarantees

- Build-time pipeline: descriptor closure → relational plan → prost binding → typed emitter renderer, four private responsibilities; not extended into public traits or SDK.
- The relational plan (tables, columns, Arrow types, nullability, parent, repeated, oneof, enum definition origin, legal names) is the single source of truth for descriptor-derived roots and descendants; Schema and emitter derive only from it — no drift among descriptor, Rust field access, and Arrow Schema.
- Roots bound by canonical FQN (two packages with the same short message name never silently mis-bind).
- No runtime descriptor interpreter, generic value tree, or string path lookup — predictable typed-decode performance and auditability.
- Only the reachable descriptor closure of bound roots is traversed; unreachable unsupported shapes don't affect bound roots (sliced scope stays local); reachable unsupported shapes fail at build time (no silent degradation).
- Name conflicts fail at build time — no table/column shadowing.
- Same Native Hook payload decoded exactly once; descriptor-derived tables and future normalized facts don't re-parse the same bytes.
- Bounded temporary spool preserves the existing "complete decode/validate before opening target" boundary; no streaming write that weakens the failure contract.

## Acceptance Evidence

- A real `.htrace` sample with value-by-value differential proving no decoded semantics lost protobuf→Parquet (not synthetic fixtures only).
- Release-build wall time, peak RSS, and Parquet bytes measurements for the full source surface.
- All existing sched, clock, loss, ordering, continuity, and overwrite behavior regressions pass.
- Fixed-result, ftrace, and other plugins can onboard root-by-root under the same contract.
